2022_25_2_a_troy_school_district_0622_sa.paragraph: Federal Awards Supplemental Information for Troy School District for the year ended June 30, 2022, issued in draft, containing three independent auditor's reports dated October 4, 2022, the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards, a reconciliation to financial statement federal revenue, notes, and the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs. Total federal expenditures for the year were $18,847,642, with accrued (deferred) revenue of $6,419,392 at June 30, 2022. Both major programs — the Special Education Cluster and the Education Stabilization Fund — received unmodified compliance opinions, with no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies, and no current-year findings; the School District qualified as a low-risk auditee.
2022_25_2_a_troy_school_district_0622_sa.page:
**What this is**
Draft single audit package (Federal Awards Supplemental Information) for Troy School District, year ended June 30, 2022, prepared for the Board of Education. All three auditor's reports are dated October 4, 2022.

**Contents and pagination**
Report on the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (1); Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters under Government Auditing Standards (2); Report on Compliance for Each Major Federal Program and on Internal Control Over Compliance under the Uniform Guidance (3-4); Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (5-8); Reconciliation of Basic Financial Statements Federal Revenue with the Schedule (9); Notes (10); Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs (11).

**Opinions and results**
Opinions on the basic financial statements (governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information) were unmodified. No internal control deficiencies rising to material weaknesses were identified, and testing disclosed no noncompliance reportable under Government Auditing Standards. The School District complied in all material respects with requirements applicable to each major federal program.

**Summary of auditor's results**

| Item | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Type of auditor's report issued | Unmodified |
| Material weaknesses (financial reporting) | No |
| Significant deficiencies (financial reporting) | None reported |
| Noncompliance material to financial statements | None reported |
| Material weaknesses (major programs) | No |
| Significant deficiencies (major programs) | None reported |
| Findings under 2 CFR 200.516(a) | No |
| Type A/type B dollar threshold | $750,000 |
| Low-risk auditee | Yes |

Major programs: Special Education Cluster (84.027, 84.173, 84.027X, 84.173X), unmodified; Education Stabilization Fund (84.425, 84.425C, 84.425D, 84.425U), unmodified. Section II (financial statement audit findings) and Section III (federal program audit findings) each report "None" for the current year.

2022_25_2_a_troy_school_district_0622_sa.verbose:
**Document and issuance**
Troy School District Federal Awards Supplemental Information for the year ended June 30, 2022, marked Draft, submitted to the Board of Education. The independent auditor's reports are each dated October 4, 2022, and the auditors state they have not performed procedures with respect to the audited financial statements subsequent to October 4, 2022.

**Auditor's reports**
The first report covers the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards required by the Uniform Guidance. The auditors audited the financial statements of the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2022, and issued a report containing unmodified opinions. In their opinion the schedule of expenditures of federal awards and the reconciliation of financial statements federal revenue with the schedule are fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole.

The second report, under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, addresses internal control over financial reporting and compliance. The auditors did not identify any deficiencies in internal control that they consider to be material weaknesses, and the results of their tests disclosed no instances of noncompliance or other matters required to be reported under Government Auditing Standards.

The third report addresses compliance for each major federal program and internal control over compliance required by the Uniform Guidance (Title 2 U.S. Code of Federal Regulations Part 200). In the auditors' opinion, the School District complied, in all material respects, with the compliance requirements identified in the OMB Compliance Supplement that could have a direct and material effect on each major federal program for the year ended June 30, 2022. No deficiencies in internal control over compliance were identified that the auditors consider material weaknesses.

2022_26_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC's required communication to the Troy School District Board of Education accompanying the audit of the basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2022, in three parts: Results of the Audit, Other Recommendations and Observations, and Informational Items. The letter reports no disagreements with management, no difficulties, and all immaterial misstatements corrected, and names the MPSERS net pension and OPEB liability estimates of $210,869,230 and $13,509,781 as the most sensitive estimates. It also flags that the Food Service Fund's fund balance exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture's three-month maximum and will require a spenddown plan filed with the Michigan Department of Education.
2022_26_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.page:
**What this is**
Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC on the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2022, dated October 5, 2022 and signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office. Structure: Results of the Audit (1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (5-6), Informational Items (7-17).

**Audit results**
Engagement letter dated June 1, 2022; planning-matters letter dated July 29, 2022; audit report and management representation letter both dated October 5, 2022. The District adopted GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, as of July 1, 2021. The most sensitive estimates were the District's shares of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB 68 and 75: $210,869,230 for pension and $13,509,781 for OPEB at June 30, 2022, from Office of Retirement Services data. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance, no significant difficulties arose, there were no disagreements with management, and management corrected all immaterial misstatements. A separate 2 CFR Part 200 report on federal programs was also issued October 5, 2022.

**Other recommendations and observations**
GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that grouped purchases individually below the capitalization threshold but above it in the aggregate belong in fixed asset records, effective for the year ending June 30, 2024. The Food Service Fund's fund balance exceeds the USDA maximum of three months of operating expenditures; a spenddown plan must go to the Michigan Department of Education.

**State funding**

| Item | 2021/2022 | 2022/2023 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target foundation allowance | $8,700 per pupil | $9,150 per pupil |
| Change | at least $171 per pupil increase (former target $8,529) | $450 per pupil increase, 5.2 percent |
| Troy foundation allowance | $9,430 per pupil, up $115 from 2021 | at target, except hold harmless districts |
| MPSERS overall contribution rate | 43 percent, up from 42 percent | 45 percent, up from 43 percent |

Net MPSERS cost to the District approximates 28 percent in both years; the total contribution rate was 11 percent when Proposal A was adopted. State retirement support received: $1,062,198 in Section 147a1, $1,841,462 in 147a2, $13,922,709 in 147c1, and $311,632 in 147e. Other 2022/2023 items: GSRP expansion of 1,300 new openings; Section 31a/At-Risk fully funded; $10,000 tuition support for future teachers and $9,600 stipends per semester for student teachers; $475 million for a school consolidation and infrastructure fund; ISD operations allocation increasing to 5.2 percent. Pupil counts blend 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring. Statewide enrollment, historically slightly under 1.5 million, fell about 10,000 per year pre-pandemic and by more than 50,000 during the pandemic. The May 2022 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference projected surpluses for 2024 and 2025; the next was set for January 2023, and most federal pandemic funding must be used by September 30, 2024.

**Fund balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000 in 2021/2022, bringing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.12 percent, roughly 9.9 weeks of operation; the statewide average at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent, roughly 10.0 weeks.

**MPSERS plan status**
At September 30, 2021 the plan's net pension liability was approximately $24.2 billion, down approximately 30 percent from $35 billion a year earlier; net OPEB liability was approximately $1.5 billion, down approximately 72 percent from $5.4 billion. The plan returned 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021, versus 5.0 percent (pension) and 4.9 percent (OPEB) the prior year.

**Upcoming standards and cybersecurity**
GASB's Financial Reporting Model Improvements project (started August 2013, exposure draft June 2020, comments closed February 2021) targets final standards by December 2023, with phased adoption at June 30, 2025 for districts with annual revenue over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under. Revenue and Expense Recognition could be issued during 2027. GASB 96 (subscription-based IT arrangements) is effective for June 30, 2023; GASB 101 (compensated absences) for June 30, 2025. The report closes with cybersecurity guidance citing the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021, signed October 2021, weak passwords such as "August2022," and PII/FERPA data handling.
2022_26_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.verbose:
**Engagement and signatories**
Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District covering the audit of the basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2022, issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC and signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The transmittal letter and the audit communications are dated October 5, 2022, and the firm extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office. The report is organized in three parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-17).

**Responsibilities, scope, and timing**
The engagement letter was dated June 1, 2022, and the planning-matters letter was dated July 29, 2022; the audit was performed according to the planned scope and timing. The audit was conducted under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 5, 2022 addressed internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. As required by 2 CFR Part 200, an audit of federal programs was also completed, with results provided to the Board in a report dated October 5, 2022. A management representation letter was obtained dated October 5, 2022.

**Significant audit findings**
Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. As described in Note 2, the School District adopted GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, with the accounting change adopted as of July 1, 2021. The auditors noted no transactions entered into during the year for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75: $210,869,230 for pension and $13,509,781 for OPEB as of June 30, 2022, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

**Other recommendations and observations**
GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 updates guidance on fixed assets, clarifying that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed it in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; the clarified guidance takes effect in the year ending June 30, 2024, and the District should review its practices and written policies. Separately, the Food Service Fund's fund balance exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District will be required to develop a spenddown plan and submit it to the Michigan Department of Education.

**School funding narrative**
The informational section is headed "School Funding - From Projected Hardships to the Largest Level of Funding Since the Start of Proposal A." It notes that pandemic-era predictions of cuts and prorations did not materialize; that in 2021/2022 the gap between base and target foundation was eliminated; that 2022/2023 brought the largest per pupil increase since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995); and that state contributions rose above constitutional minimums for special education and for retirement system cost reduction.

**2021/2022 state funding**
All schools were moved to the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap, and all schools including hold harmless districts received an increase of at least $171 per pupil from the former target level of $8,529. Progress was also made on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP). Based on these changes, Troy School District's foundation allowance per pupil was $9,430, an increase of $115 from the 2021 funding level.

**2022/2023 state funding**
Key highlights listed include: increasing the target foundation allowance by $450 per pupil to $9,150, a 5.2 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving the $450 increase; continuing the traditional blended pupil count with 90 percent weighting for the October 2022 count and 10 percent weighting for the February 2022 count; continuing increases in special education cost reimbursement, with 2022 and 2023 marking the first time since the start of Proposal A that special education allocations exceeded state constitutional minimum levels; increasing GSRP funding to create 1,300 new openings for students; fully funding Section 31a/At-Risk programs, previously subject to proration; increasing career and technical education funding; increasing student mental health funding; teacher recruitment resources including $10,000 in tuition support for future teachers, $9,600 stipends per semester for student teachers, and "Grow Your Own" programs; expansion of before- and after-school programs focused on at-risk and economically disadvantaged students; dedicated school safety funding for school resource officers, intervention systems, and a school safety commission; increased retirement system contributions; allocation of $475 million of state aid funds for a school consolidation and infrastructure fund, described as the first such state allocation; and an ISD operations allocation increasing to 5.2 percent to mirror the foundation increase.

**Federal resources and outlook**
Federal assistance has come in waves since March 2020, with most funding ending in 2024; ARP ESSER III and Section 11t carry more restrictions than earlier relief. The window for using the majority of those funds closes by September 30, 2024. The most recent Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference, finalized in May 2022, projected a healthy School Aid Fund with a 2022 surplus carrying into 2023 and surpluses expected for 2024 and 2025; the next conference was scheduled for January 2023. Risks identified include inflation and a potential recession, noting that the 5.2 percent foundation increase is higher than any seen under Proposal A but could be consumed by higher operating costs.

**2022 funding implications for the District**
Listed items include the 2021/2022 foundation allowance changes above; the ESSER programs, with ESSER III made available during 2021/2022 in two components, ESSER III formula and ESSER III equalization (also known as 11t, authorized by Section 11t of PA 48 of 2021), federally funded under the American Rescue Plan and scheduled to end during 2024; the pupil membership blend for 2021/2022 returning to 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring after the 2020/2021 "super blend"; summer school and learning assistance funding through ESSER II and state appropriations, with costs and revenue split between the 2021 and 2022 fiscal years; and MPSERS costs for 2021/2022, where the overall contribution rate increased to 43 percent from 42 percent with net cost to the District approximating 28 percent. State support is provided through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act; the District received $1,062,198 in 147a1, $1,841,462 in 147a2, $13,922,709 in 147c1, and $311,632 of 147e funding.

**2023 funding implications for the District**
The school aid package, described as the largest ever, was agreed before the start of the District's 2022/2023 fiscal year, though a budget amendment is likely because the state budget passed after districts had to adopt original budgets. All districts are at the target foundation allowance of $9,150 except a few hold harmless districts. Pupil count uses 90 percent of the fall 2022 count and 10 percent of the spring 2022 count. For 2023 the MPSERS overall contribution rate increases to 45 percent from 43 percent, with net cost to the District continuing at up to approximately 28 percent; by comparison, the total contribution rate was 11 percent when Proposal A was adopted. Beginning in 2021/2022 the State increased funding of its share of special education costs by 3 percent of those costs, continuing in 2022/2023 with a reduction in the amount of foundation allowance credited against the State's required support.

**Pupil count trends**
Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, declining about 10,000 per year before the pandemic and decreasing in excess of 50,000 during the pandemic. Some recovery is estimated but not to pre-pandemic levels.

**Grants management and budgeting**
The report describes increased workload and grants management risk from ESSER, GEER, and CRF programs, touching superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, and facilities, and recommends continued assessment of compliance risks moving into the 2023 fiscal year.

**Fund balance**
During the 2021/2022 school year the School District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would equal approximately 10.0 weeks of average operating costs. The School District's fund balance percentage is 19.12 percent and equals approximately 9.9 weeks of operation.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities**
The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2021 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $24.2 billion, a decrease of approximately 30 percent from the reported $35 billion at September 30, 2020, driven largely by net investment gains; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 compared with 5.0 percent for the year ended September 30, 2020. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021, down from $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, a decrease of approximately 72 percent, attributed to the 27.2 percent return compared with 4.9 percent the prior year. Because markets declined after the valuation date, the net liabilities are expected to increase significantly next year.

**Future GASB standards**
The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013, with an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" issued June 2020 and a comment period that ended February 2021 (Plante & Moran submitted comments); final standards are targeted for December 2023. Proposed changes include additional MD&A information, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budget, terminology changes replacing "revenue" with "inflows of resources" and "expenditures" with "outflows of resources," and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" using a 12-month conversion window rather than the current 60-day rule. Phased adoption would apply at the year ending June 30, 2025 for districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under $75 million. A related project, "Revenue and Expense Recognition," released as preliminary views in June 2020, could produce a standard during 2027. GASB Statement No. 96, Subscription-based Information Technology Arrangements, is effective for the District's June 30, 2023 financial statements and mirrors GASB 87 by requiring a right-to-use subscription asset and subscription liability measured at the net present value of extended payment terms, with fund-level expenditures reclassified as debt service payments. GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requires a full-accrual liability for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the financial statement date, and removes the gross additions/reductions and liquidating-fund disclosure requirements.

**Cybersecurity**
Education remains a top target for ransomware; the "K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021" was signed into law in October 2021. The report warns that easily guessed passwords such as "August2022" and phishing emails make the human element the weakest link, asks whether staff are aware of phishing risks, where district data resides, and whether PII or FERPA-protected data is stored on file-sharing sites, flash drives, or personal email, and suggests an external vulnerability assessment.
